name: Python
title: Python from the first line
intro: Python reads almost like plain English, which makes it a gentle first language and a serious everyday tool: it runs websites, science, spreadsheets-on-steroids and the scripts that glue other programs together. These lessons go from your first print to writing small classes. Every example shows exactly what it prints. To run code yourself, install Python 3 from python.org and type python (or py on Windows) in a terminal, or save the code in a file ending in .py and run python file.py.

sections.p: print shows whatever you put between its brackets. Text goes in quotes; single and double quotes mean the same thing. Each print starts a new line.
sections.code:
print("Hello, squirrel!")
print('Nuts are ready.')
print(7)

sections.p: Separate values with commas and print puts a space between them. Text in quotes is a string; numbers need no quotes.
sections.code:
print("I have", 3, "acorns")
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")

sections.p: Everything after a # is a comment: Python ignores it. Comments are notes for people reading the code, including you next month.
sections.code:
# This line does nothing.
print("Only this shows")  # a comment can follow code too

sections.p: Inside a string, \n starts a new line and \t is a tab. To put a quote inside, use the other kind of quote around the string.
sections.code:
print("one\ntwo")
print("She said 'hi'")

practice.why: Commas between values become single spaces, and the quotes are not printed.
The first line is a comment because it starts with #, so it never runs.
sep sets what goes between the values; an empty string means nothing at all.

practice.q: Which line is a valid string with an apostrophe in it?
practice.why: Double quotes around the text let the single quote inside be an ordinary character.
\n inside a string is a newline, so b lands on the next line.
end="" stops print from adding its usual newline, so the next print carries on the same line.
sep can be a newline, so the two values land on separate lines.

lessons.title: Variables and types
lessons.summary: Names for values, and the four basic kinds of value.

sections.p: A variable is a name that points at a value. = means “make this name point at this value”, not “is equal to”. You can point the name somewhere else later.
sections.code:
nuts = 5
print(nuts)
nuts = nuts + 2
print(nuts)

sections.p: Whole numbers are int, numbers with a decimal point are float, text is str, and True/False are bool. type() tells you which one you have.
sections.code:
print(type(42))
print(type(4.2))
print(type("42"))
print(type(True))

sections.p: int(), float() and str() turn one type into another. This matters because "2" + "3" joins text while 2 + 3 adds numbers.
sections.code:
print("2" + "3")
print(int("2") + int("3"))
print("Score: " + str(10))

sections.p: Put an f before the quotes and anything in {braces} is filled in from your variables. This is the everyday way to build a message.
sections.code:
name = "Hazel"
age = 3
print(f"{name} is {age} years old")
print(f"Next year: {age + 1}")
sections.out:
Hazel is 3 years old
Next year: 4

sections.p: Names use letters, digits and underscores, and cannot start with a digit. Case matters: Nuts and nuts are different. Python style is lowercase words joined by underscores: nuts_buried.

practice.why: x starts at 4; the second line takes the current 4, doubles it and points x at 8.
Both are strings, so + joins them end to end.
The decimal point makes 3.0 a float, even though it is a whole number.
The f before the quotes makes {tree} get replaced by the variable's value.

practice.q: Which is a valid variable name?
practice.why: Names cannot start with a digit or contain spaces or hyphens; underscores and later digits are fine.
b was pointed at the value 1. Moving a to 9 afterwards does not move b.
int chops 3.9 down to 3; float("2") is 2.0; 3 + 2.0 is the float 5.0.
True and False are bool values.

sections.p: The usual operators work as on a calculator. Note that / always gives a float, even when the division is exact.
sections.code:
print(7 + 3)
print(7 - 3)
print(7 * 3)
print(6 / 3)

sections.p: // divides and drops the fraction. % gives what is left over. Together they answer “how many full groups, and how many spare?”.
sections.code:
acorns = 17
print(acorns // 5)   # full bags of 5
print(acorns % 5)    # left over

sections.p: ** raises to a power. Python follows maths order: powers first, then * / // %, then + -. Brackets go first of all.
sections.code:
print(2 ** 3)
print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)

sections.p: round, abs, min and max are built in. Shortcuts like += update a variable in place.
sections.code:
print(round(3.14159, 2))
print(abs(-8))
print(max(4, 9, 2))
total = 10
total += 5
print(total)

practice.why: / always produces a float.
4 fits into 14 three times (12) with 2 left over.
// keeps only the whole part of 3.5.
Multiplication comes first: 2 * 3 = 6, then 1 + 6.
n *= 4 is short for n = n * 4.

practice.q: How would you test whether a number n is even?
practice.why: An even number leaves no remainder when divided by 2.
** raises to a power: 2 to the 4th is 16.
round goes to the nearest whole number, abs drops the sign, max picks the largest.

lessons.title: Working with strings
lessons.summary: Indexing, slicing, length and string methods.

sections.p: A string is a sequence of characters, numbered from 0. Square brackets pick one out. Negative numbers count from the end.
sections.code:
word = "squirrel"
print(word[0])
print(word[3])
print(word[-1])
print(len(word))

sections.p: word[a:b] takes characters from position a up to, but not including, b. Leave a side empty to mean “from the start” or “to the end”.
sections.code:
word = "squirrel"
print(word[0:3])
print(word[3:])
print(word[:-1])

sections.p: Strings come with tools called with a dot. They return a new string; the original never changes (strings are immutable).
sections.code:
s = "  Pine Cone  "
print(s.strip())
print(s.strip().upper())
print(s.strip().replace("Cone", "Nut"))
print("a,b,c".split(","))
sections.out:
Pine Cone
PINE CONE
Pine Nut
['a', 'b', 'c']

sections.p: in checks whether one string appears inside another. find gives the position, or -1 if it is missing.
sections.code:
print("nut" in "chestnut")
print("chestnut".find("nut"))
print("chestnut".find("pea"))

practice.why: Counting starts at 0: f is 0, o is 1.
-1 is the last character (t); -2 is the one before it.
Positions 2, 3 and 4; the slice stops before 5.
upper() returns a new string, but nothing keeps it. s itself never changes.
The space counts as a character.
split() with no argument splits on whitespace and returns a list.
c-h-e-s-t are positions 0–4; nut starts at 5.
strip removes the spaces first; then replace swaps Pine for Oak.

lessons.title: Making decisions
lessons.summary: if, elif, else, comparisons and logic.

sections.p: if runs a block only when a condition is true. The block is the indented lines after the colon; indentation is how Python knows where it ends. Four spaces is the norm.
sections.code:
nuts = 12
if nuts > 10:
    print("Enough for winter")
print("Done counting")

sections.p: Add elif for more conditions and else for everything left. Python checks them top to bottom and runs only the first match.
== equal, != not equal, < > <= >=. Remember: one = assigns, two compare. Combine conditions with and, or, not.
sections.code:
age = 15
print(age >= 13 and age <= 19)
print(age == 15)
print(not age > 20)

sections.p: Empty things count as false: 0, "", [], None. Almost everything else counts as true, so if name: means “if name is not empty”.

practice.why: 7 > 5 is true, so only the if block runs.
Only the first true branch runs. n > 10 is already true, so elif is never checked.
== compares values, and 3 and 3.0 are the same number.
not True is False, and True and False is False.
An empty list counts as false.
Python refuses assignment inside an if condition, which catches a very common slip.
n is not out of range, so the first if is false; both parts of the elif are true.
0 counts as false, so or moves on and gives the next value.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: for, range, while, break and continue.

sections.p: A for loop runs its block once for each item in a sequence. A string is a sequence of characters.
sections.code:
for letter in "nut":
    print(letter)

sections.p: range(n) counts 0, 1, … up to but not including n. range(a, b) starts at a; a third number sets the step.
while repeats as long as its condition is true. Make sure something inside changes, or the loop never ends.
sections.code:
stash = 1
while stash < 20:
    stash = stash * 3
print(stash)

sections.p: break leaves the loop at once. continue skips to the next round.
A common pattern: start a total at zero and add to it inside the loop.
sections.code:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 5):
    total += n
print(total)

practice.q: How many lines does this print?
practice.why: range(4) gives 0, 1, 2, 3: four rounds.
range(2, 5) starts at 2 and stops before 5.
The loop stops as soon as n < 3 is false, which first happens at 3.
The loop stops at o before printing it.

practice.code:
s = 0
for i in range(5):
    s += i
print(s)
practice.why: 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. range(5) never reaches 5.
Start at 5, step −2, stop before 0.
continue skips the even numbers before print runs.
1 → 2 → 4 → 8; once n is 8 the while test fails.

sections.p: A list holds several values in order, inside square brackets. Indexing and slicing work just like strings.
sections.code:
trees = ["oak", "beech", "pine"]
print(trees[0])
print(trees[-1])
print(len(trees))

sections.p: Unlike strings, lists are mutable: you can change them in place.
sections.code:
trees = ["oak", "beech"]
trees.append("pine")
trees[0] = "elm"
trees.remove("beech")
print(trees)

sections.p: Loop straight over the items. sorted() gives a new sorted list; .sort() sorts the list itself. enumerate hands you the position too.
sections.code:
scores = [7, 2, 9]
print(sorted(scores))
print(sum(scores), max(scores))
for i, s in enumerate(scores):
    print(i, s)

sections.p: A compact way to build one list from another: [expression for item in sequence if condition].
sections.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
squares = [n * n for n in nums]
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
print(squares)
print(evens)

sections.p: Assigning a list to a second name does not copy it. Both names point at the same list, so a change through one shows through the other. Use .copy() for a separate list.
sections.code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
c = a.copy()
a.append(3)
print(b)
print(c)

practice.why: Index 1 is the second item.
append adds one item, and here that item is the list [3].
range(3) is 0, 1, 2; each is doubled.
a and b are two names for the same list.
sorted() returns a new list and leaves the original alone.
Positions 1 and 2; the slice stops before 3.
.sort() changes the list itself, unlike sorted() which returns a new one.

practice.code: print([n for n in range(6) if n % 2 == 1])
practice.why: The if keeps only the odd numbers from range(6).

lessons.title: Dictionaries, tuples and sets
lessons.summary: Look things up by key; fixed pairs; unique items.

sections.p: A dictionary maps keys to values, like words to definitions. Look up, add or change a value with its key in square brackets.
sections.code:
stash = {"acorn": 12, "hazelnut": 5}
print(stash["acorn"])
stash["walnut"] = 2
stash["acorn"] -= 1
print(stash)

sections.p: Asking for a key that is not there raises a KeyError. .get() returns a default instead, and in checks first.
.items() gives key and value together. Dictionaries keep the order you inserted things.
A tuple is like a list in round brackets that cannot be changed. It is handy for fixed groups, and for returning several values at once. Unpack it into separate names.
sections.code:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x + y)

sections.p: A set keeps each value once. It is the quickest way to drop duplicates or test membership.
sections.code:
seen = set(["oak", "pine", "oak", "elm", "pine"])
print(len(seen))
print("elm" in seen)

practice.why: The key "b" maps to 2.
Assigning to an existing key replaces its value; there is still one key.
get returns the default you gave when the key is missing.
A set keeps each value once: {1, 2, 3}.

options: A TypeError: tuples cannot be changed
practice.answer: A TypeError: tuples cannot be changed
practice.why: Tuples are immutable. Build a new tuple instead.

practice.code:
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a
print(a, b)
practice.why: The right side builds the tuple (2, 1) first, then unpacks it, so the swap works.
in checks keys; get returns the default −1 when elm is missing.

practice.code:
point = (10, 20)
x, y = point
print(x * y)
practice.why: Unpacking fills x and y from the tuple; 10 × 20 = 200.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: def, parameters, return values and scope.

sections.p: A function is a named block you can run whenever you need it. def defines it; calling it by name with brackets runs it.
sections.code:
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Hazel")
greet("Rowan")

sections.p: return sends a value back to whoever called the function. A function with no return gives back None.
sections.code:
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

big = area(4, 5)
print(big)
print(area(2, 3) + 1)

sections.p: Give a parameter a default and callers can leave it out. Callers can also name arguments, which keeps long calls readable.
sections.code:
def bag(nuts, size=10):
    return nuts // size

print(bag(35))
print(bag(35, size=5))

sections.p: Variables made inside a function are local: they exist only while it runs and do not touch names outside. Pass values in as parameters and get results out with return.
sections.code:
count = 1

def bump():
    count = 100
    return count

print(bump())
print(count)

practice.why: double(3) is 6, and double(6) is 12.

practice.code:
def f():
    print("hi")

x = f()
print(x)
practice.why: Calling f prints hi. f has no return, so x is None.
The first call uses the default b=2; the second passes 5.

practice.code:
x = 5
def change():
    x = 10
change()
print(x)
practice.why: x = 10 inside the function makes a separate local x.

practice.code:
def first_two(word):
    return word[:2]
    print("unreached")

print(first_two("pine"))
practice.why: return ends the function immediately; the line after it never runs.

practice.code:
def pair(a, b=1):
    return a, a + b

x, y = pair(4)
print(x, y)
practice.why: Returning two values makes a tuple that unpacks into x and y; b defaults to 1.
The named argument count=3 overrides the default.

lessons.title: Errors and exceptions
lessons.summary: Reading tracebacks and handling problems with try.

sections.p: When something goes wrong Python stops and prints a traceback. Read its last line first: it names the error and gives a short reason. The lines above show where it happened.
sections.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "stash.py", line 2, in <module>
    print(stash["pecan"])
KeyError: 'pecan'

sections.p: SyntaxError: the code is not valid Python (missing colon or bracket). IndentationError: the spaces at the start of a line do not line up. NameError: a name is used before it exists, often a typo. TypeError: an operation on the wrong kind of value, like "3" + 4. ValueError: right type, bad value, like int("abc"). IndexError/KeyError: a position or key that is not there. ZeroDivisionError: dividing by zero.
Wrap risky code in try. If a matching error happens, the except block runs instead of the program crashing.
else runs when no error happened; finally always runs. raise signals an error yourself when a value makes no sense.
sections.out:
Problem: need at least one squirrel
Checked

practice.why: int accepts a string, so the type is fine; the value cannot be read as a number.
You cannot add a str and an int; convert one first.
prnt is a name Python has never seen; it is a typo for print.
Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError, which the except block catches.

practice.code:
try:
    x = [1, 2][5]
except IndexError:
    x = 0
finally:
    print("end")
print(x)
practice.why: The IndexError is caught and x set to 0; finally prints end; then x is printed.
int succeeds, so else runs and adds 1; except is skipped.
Dictionaries raise KeyError for a missing key; IndexError is for sequences.

lessons.title: Modules and files
lessons.summary: import, the standard library, reading and writing files.

sections.p: Python ships with a large standard library. import brings a module in; use its contents with a dot, or import names directly with from.
sections.code:
import math
from datetime import date

print(math.sqrt(81))
print(math.pi > 3)
print(date(2024, 3, 1).strftime("%A"))

sections.p: open(name, "w") opens a file for writing (replacing it). The with statement closes the file for you when the block ends, even after an error.
sections.code:
with open("nuts.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("acorn\n")
    f.write("hazelnut\n")
print("saved")

sections.p: Open with "r" (the default) to read. Looping over a file gives one line at a time, each ending in a newline, which .strip() removes. Use "a" to add to the end instead of replacing.
sections.code:
with open("nuts.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("acorn\nhazelnut\n")

with open("nuts.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip().title())

sections.p: Any .py file is a module. Save functions in helpers.py and import helpers from a file next to it. Code under if __name__ == "__main__": runs only when the file is run directly, not when it is imported.

practice.why: floor rounds down to the nearest whole number.

practice.q: Why use `with open(...) as f:` rather than plain `f = open(...)`?
options: It is the only way to write
practice.why: Leaving the with block always closes the file, even if an error happens inside.

practice.q: Which mode adds to the end of an existing file?
practice.why: a is append. w empties the file first; r only reads; x fails if the file exists.
sqrt returns a float, 4.0, and 4.0 + 1 is 5.0.

practice.code:
with open("t.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("a\nb\n")
with open("t.txt") as f:
    print(len(f.readlines()))
practice.why: The file holds two lines, a and b; readlines returns a list of both.
ceil rounds up to the next whole number.

practice.code:
with open("note.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("oak")
with open("note.txt") as f:
    print(f.read().upper())
practice.why: read() pulls the whole file as one string; upper makes it OAK.

lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.summary: Bundling data with the functions that use it.

sections.p: A class is a blueprint; each object made from it carries its own data. __init__ runs when an object is created and stores values on self, the object being built.
sections.code:
class Squirrel:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.nuts = 0

hazel = Squirrel("Hazel")
rowan = Squirrel("Rowan")
hazel.nuts = 4
print(hazel.name, hazel.nuts)
print(rowan.name, rowan.nuts)

sections.p: Functions defined inside a class are methods. Their first parameter is always self, and Python fills it in for you.
Define __str__ to choose what print shows for your object.
A class can build on another. The new class gets every method of its parent and can add or replace some.

practice.why: Each object keeps its own n: 1 and 2.
Each call to inc adds 1 to the same object's v.

options: The object the method was called on
practice.answer: The object the method was called on
practice.why: c.inc() runs inc with self set to c.
B inherits hi from A unchanged; pass just means the body is empty.
print uses __str__ when the class defines it.
Bird replaces speak; the parent's version is not used.
add returns the new total each time: 0+2 then 2+3.
